burnout-signs-high-performers.meta_title: 7 Signs of Burnout High Performers Ignore | Johnny Durán
burnout-signs-high-performers.meta_description: You're still performing. But something's off. These are the 7 early signs of burnout that high-achieving leaders dismiss — and what they actually mean.
burnout-signs-high-performers.hero_img_alt: Burnout signs high performers should recognise
burnout-signs-high-performers.label: Burnout · Performance · Leaders
burnout-signs-high-performers.cta_body: If what you read landed somewhere real, let's talk. One honest conversation can shift more than six months of doing it alone.

content.text: The most dangerous version of burnout in high performers isn't the one that puts you in bed for a week. It's the one that shows up quietly while you're still hitting your targets, still leading your team, still performing — because that version is almost impossible to diagnose until something breaks. If you're reading this, you probably already suspect something's off. The burnout signs high performers experience look different from the textbook version, and this article is for those who need the unvarnished version.

I've worked with founders, executives, and leaders across Europe and Latin America from my base in Barcelona. The pattern is remarkably consistent: by the time they reach out, they've been carrying a version of burnout for 12 to 18 months. They didn't call it that. They called it "a demanding quarter," "a rough patch," or "just tired." Here's how to tell the difference.
The 7 Signs of Burnout That High Performers Miss
1. Persistent Flatness — Not Sadness, Just Nothing

This isn't depression in the clinical sense. It's closer to a greying out. Things that used to excite you — new projects, travel, dinner with people you like — feel muted. You attend, you perform, you leave. The enthusiasm is gone, not because you're miserable, but because you're running on fumes and the emotional range starts to narrow. Executive burnout symptoms often begin here, long before the more dramatic signs appear.
2. Decision Fatigue That Hits Earlier Each Day

You used to be sharp at 10am. Now you're second-guessing yourself by 9. Small decisions feel disproportionately heavy. What to prioritise, who to respond to first, whether a message is worth sending — all of it takes more energy than it should. This is a classic sign of burnout at work: the cognitive load of everyday decisions starts to feel like a full-body effort.
3. A Quiet but Growing Cynicism

The work you once found meaningful starts to feel hollow. You find yourself more sarcastic in meetings, less patient with the idealism of others, quicker to dismiss things you'd previously have engaged with. This isn't you becoming more realistic. It's your nervous system protecting itself from further investment in things it no longer has the capacity to care about.
4. Tension That Lives in Your Body

Tight jaw. Chronic shoulder tension. The feeling that you wake up already braced for something. Your body has been holding stress for so long it's forgotten what it feels like not to. Most high performers I work with are so focused on cognitive output they stop noticing their physical state altogether — until something forces them to.
5. You've Lost the Plot on Why You're Doing Any of This

Not in a dramatic existential crisis way. More like: you used to have a clear internal answer to "why does this matter?" and now when you reach for it, there's nothing there. Burnout vs tiredness is often most clearly distinguished here — tiredness resolves with rest; this kind of hollowness doesn't.
6. Working More But Achieving Less

Your hours are the same or longer. But your output — and more importantly, your sense of quality — has declined. You finish less. You restart more. The cognitive bandwidth that used to carry you through a complex project now stalls halfway in. This isn't laziness. It's a depleted system trying to do precision work without the fuel.
7. Emotional Unavailability — Everywhere

Not just at home, though that's usually where it's most visible. You find it harder to genuinely connect — with your team, your partner, even with yourself. You're present in the room but absent in the conversation. Partners often describe this phase as "you're here but you're not here." They're right.
Burnout doesn't arrive as a collapse.
content.highlight: It arrives as a slow loss of yourself.

content.text: Why High Performers Miss These Signs

The answer is identity. When your sense of self is tightly woven into your performance — your output, your results, your ability to handle pressure — acknowledging burnout feels like admitting you're broken. So instead, you reclassify it. The flatness becomes "being realistic." The cynicism becomes "having high standards." The exhaustion becomes "dedication."

This is the trap. And it's not a character flaw — it's a structural problem with how most high-achievers are trained to relate to themselves. Burnout recovery for this group starts not with better habits, but with honest recognition of what's actually happening.
"The willingness to perform is not evidence that you're okay. It's often evidence of the opposite."
Why Rest Alone Won't Fix This

Here's what most people get wrong about executive burnout symptoms: they think the prescription is rest. Take a holiday. Sleep more. Disconnect for a few days. And then they come back from the holiday feeling exactly the same, which is demoralising, because if rest doesn't fix it, what will?

The answer lies in understanding what burnout actually is at a physiological level. Chronic stress doesn't just tire you out — it dysregulates your nervous system. Your body is running in a low-grade threat response. Rest helps, but it doesn't discharge the accumulated tension or reset the internal operating system that's been running on adrenaline. That requires different work — deliberate, specific, and more internal than most productivity frameworks acknowledge.

If you want to go deeper on what's happening under the surface, this article on burnout in Barcelona and the role of environment covers the nervous system dimension in detail. You can also read the WHO's official classification of burnout as an occupational phenomenon — their framing is useful precisely because it separates burnout from depression and anxiety.
What Actually Helps
The sequence matters. You can't strategy your way out of burnout. You can't optimise your way out. The sequence for genuine burnout recovery looks like this:

items.text: Before strategy, before goals, before any kind of redesign — your nervous system needs to come out of survival mode. Breathwork, somatic practices, structured stillness. Not as luxuries, as prerequisites.
Not a productivity audit. An energy audit. What is genuinely restoring you? What is depleting you that you've been calling "part of the job"?

items.strong: Address the source, not the symptoms.
items.text: Burnout is usually a misalignment problem — between how you're living and what you actually need. No amount of sleep or holiday will fix a misaligned operating system.

items.strong: Work with someone who has done this before.
items.text: Not a productivity coach. Someone who understands the nervous system, the identity dimension, and the specific pressures of high-performance environments.

content.text: If you're seeing yourself in this list — if three or more of these signs are familiar — I'd encourage you to take it seriously. Not because you're broken, but because you've been carrying something heavy for a long time and there's a more sustainable version of the performance you're reaching for. You can explore how I work with clients or start with a conversation.

stress-insomnia-leaders.meta_title: Can't Sleep From Stress? What Your Body Is Telling You | Johnny Durán
stress-insomnia-leaders.meta_description: Waking at 3am with a racing mind isn't insomnia — it's data. Here's what stress-related sleep problems actually signal, and how to address the source.
stress-insomnia-leaders.hero_img_alt: Stress insomnia and sleep problems in leaders and high performers
stress-insomnia-leaders.label: Sleep · Stress · Recovery
stress-insomnia-leaders.h1_after: And What Your Body Is Actually Telling You
stress-insomnia-leaders.cta_body: If what you read landed somewhere real, let's talk. One honest conversation can shift more than six months of doing it alone.

content.text: You can't sleep from stress. You know this. It's 3am, your mind is running a full board meeting without you, and the harder you try to shut it down, the louder it gets. You've Googled "sleep problems high performers" enough times to know you're not alone. What you haven't found yet is an honest explanation for what's actually happening — and why the standard advice keeps failing you.

I work with founders and executives across Europe, and the stress insomnia pattern is one of the most consistent things I encounter. It's also one of the most misdiagnosed. Because what most people are dealing with isn't a sleep problem. It's a nervous system problem that shows up at night — because that's the only time you've stopped performing long enough for it to surface.
The 3am Club: What's Actually Happening

Here's the physiology, without the textbook version. When you're under chronic stress, your body runs elevated cortisol — the hormone that, among other things, keeps you alert and ready to respond to threats. The problem is that modern high-performance stress isn't a lion chasing you. It's a calendar that never clears, a team that needs things, a business with a thousand open loops. The cortisol has nowhere to go. So at night, when the cognitive busyness slows, the body's arousal system is still running.

Waking between 2am and 4am is particularly common in this pattern — it corresponds to a natural cortisol rise that, in a regulated nervous system, happens gently and helps you transition back into sleep. In a chronically stressed system, that rise is exaggerated. Sleep problems from stress aren't about not being tired enough. You're exhausted. The system just can't switch off.
"Your body isn't broken. It's doing exactly what a body does when it's been running on survival for too long."
The Performance Cost Nobody Talks About Honestly

Sleep deprivation in high-performers is often normalised as a badge of commitment. What it actually does, according to research from sleep scientist Matthew Walker and his team, is significantly impair cognitive function even after just one or two nights of disrupted sleep. For leaders specifically, the cost shows up in:

items.text: Sleep-deprived brains are measurably worse at risk assessment and favour short-term, impulsive choices over considered strategy.
The amygdala — your threat-response centre — becomes overactive. Everything feels slightly more dangerous, more urgent, more personal than it actually is.
Deep problem-solving and pattern recognition both depend on consolidated sleep. Without it, you're working with a significantly reduced toolkit.
Stress hormones that aren't metabolised during sleep accumulate. The tension you're carrying in your body has nowhere to discharge.

content.text: The problem isn't that you can't sleep.
Why Sleep Hygiene Advice Doesn't Work for You

No screen time before bed. Consistent sleep schedule. Cool room. No caffeine after 2pm. You've heard all of it. Some of you have tried all of it. And it helps — marginally. Because sleep hygiene addresses the conditions for sleep. It doesn't address the state your nervous system is in when it tries to sleep.

Think of it this way: if you've been running a car engine at high revs all day, you can't just turn off the ignition and expect the engine to cool instantly. There's heat, pressure, momentum that needs to dissipate. Your nervous system works the same way. The protocol of how you sleep matters far less than the state you're in before you try to sleep — and that state is determined by what's happened to your stress response across the entire day.
3 Things That Actually Address the Source
1. Discharge the day before you try to close it

This is not meditation (though that helps). This is about giving your nervous system a specific signal that the threat-response is no longer required. Physical movement — a walk, light exercise, breathwork — metabolises the cortisol and adrenaline that have built up during the day. This is the step most people skip entirely, going from work straight to screen straight to bed and wondering why their brain won't cooperate.
2. Close your open loops before you lie down

The mind runs at night on unresolved commitments. A brief five-minute capture practice — write down everything that's on your mental stack, what needs doing tomorrow, what you're worried about — externalises the cognitive load. Your brain stops rehearsing because it has evidence the information is safe. This is simpler and more effective than most people expect.
3. Address the chronic stress, not just the nights

This is the work nobody wants to hear, but it's the only one that produces lasting change. If your nervous system is running in a chronic stress pattern — if your baseline is elevated, if rest doesn't feel restorative even when you get it — then you need to address that pattern directly. How you sleep better under pressure isn't ultimately a sleep question. It's a question about what level of pressure your system is carrying, and whether that's sustainable.

If you want to understand the full picture of what's driving your sleep disruption, this article on burnout signs in high performers covers the upstream causes. And if you'd like to work on this directly, you can read about how I approach this kind of work in the method section.

chronic-stress-focus-performance.meta_title: How Chronic Stress Drains Your Edge | Johnny Durán
chronic-stress-focus-performance.meta_description: Chronic stress doesn't announce itself. It just makes your decisions slower, your thinking cloudier, and your work feel heavier every week. Here's what's happening — and how to reverse it.
chronic-stress-focus-performance.hero_img_alt: Chronic stress affecting performance and focus in leaders
chronic-stress-focus-performance.label: Stress · Clarity · Focus
chronic-stress-focus-performance.cta_body: If what you read landed somewhere real, let's talk. One honest conversation can shift more than six months of doing it alone.

content.text: Chronic stress affecting performance is rarely dramatic. Nobody crashes. Nobody calls it quits. What happens instead is subtler and, in many ways, more dangerous: a slow, almost imperceptible erosion of the qualities that made you effective in the first place. Your thinking gets cloudier. Your decisions get heavier. Your work gets slower. And because it happens gradually, you adapt your expectations downward without realising you're doing it.

I've worked with some remarkably capable people from my base in Barcelona — founders scaling companies, executives managing complex teams, professionals carrying significant responsibility. And the most common thread in those who've been running under chronic stress isn't breakdown. It's a quiet, steady decline in what stress and focus researchers call cognitive bandwidth. Your edge. The thing that makes you, at your best, genuinely exceptional at what you do.
High Performers Don't Collapse — They Corrode

The popular image of stress-related breakdown — the dramatic exit, the hospitalisation, the total loss of function — affects a small fraction of people who don't manage chronic stress. The more common outcome is the one nobody talks about, because it's invisible from the outside and easy to rationalise from the inside.

You start arriving at decisions that feel strangely hard. You find yourself rereading the same email three times. Your thinking, which used to feel fast and clear, now feels like wading through something thick. Research from the Harvard Business Review on stress and executive performance consistently shows that sustained stress doesn't just deplete energy — it actively impairs the very cognitive functions that leaders rely on most.
"The problem isn't the workload. It's what the workload is doing to your internal operating system."
The 5 Performance Metrics Chronic Stress Kills First
Stress affecting decision making shows up in predictable ways. These are the five capabilities that deteriorate earliest in high-performers under chronic stress load:

items.text: The prefrontal cortex — your brain's planning and reasoning centre — is the first area to be compromised by elevated cortisol. Long-horizon thinking becomes difficult. You default to short-term, reactive responses even when the situation calls for something more considered.

Chronic stress makes your threat-detection system hypersensitive. Things that aren't particularly dangerous start to register as urgent. Your risk assessment skews toward catastrophe, and your decisions — financial, relational, operational — reflect that distortion.

Novel solutions require cognitive flexibility: the ability to hold multiple possibilities simultaneously, connect unrelated concepts, step back from the obvious path. Stress narrows that field. You default to known solutions, familiar patterns, the route you've taken before — even when the situation needs something new.

The capacity to read a room, regulate your own responses, and genuinely connect with your team depends on the same neural resources that stress depletes. Irritability, impatience, and the inability to track what other people actually need are all downstream effects of a stressed nervous system.

Healthy high-performers can take a hit — a bad quarter, a difficult conversation, an unexpected setback — and bounce back within hours or days. Under chronic stress, that recovery window extends dramatically. You're still processing last week's crisis when the next one arrives.

content.text: Productivity hacks
content.highlight: don't work on a depleted system.

content.text: Why Stress Management Advice Doesn't Work

Most stress management for executives focuses on tools: time-blocking, delegation, meditation apps, better calendar hygiene. Some of this is genuinely useful in a regulated system. None of it is sufficient in a chronically dysregulated one, and here's why: when you're running on sustained stress, the problem isn't the strategy. It's the state from which you're executing the strategy.

Think about it this way. If your decision-making is impaired by chronic stress, then your decisions about how to manage your stress will also be impaired. You'll pick the solutions that feel manageable within your current bandwidth — which tend to be the ones that require the least disruption and produce the shallowest results. The hard work gets deferred. The system keeps running hot.
The Sequence That Actually Works

items.text: Before goals, before optimisation, before any redesign of your working life — your nervous system needs to come down from its chronic activation state. This is not a luxury. It's the prerequisite for everything else to work.

Once your system is less activated, you regain access to your actual intelligence. What do you want? What are you actually building? What is non-negotiable and what has been assumed? These questions become answerable in ways they simply aren't under high stress load.

Only once you have a regulated nervous system and genuine clarity do the tools of performance — structure, habits, systems — have something solid to build on. Applied in this order, they compound. Applied in the wrong order, they wear you out.

content.text: If you're noticing the signs described here — the cloudiness, the heavy decisions, the loss of the edge you used to rely on — the article on burnout signs in high performers maps the fuller picture of what this trajectory looks like over time. And if you want to understand how I work with this specifically, you can read about the approach I take with the leaders I work with.

always-irritable-burnout.meta_title: Always Irritable? It's Burnout, Not Your Personality | Johnny Durán
always-irritable-burnout.meta_description: If you're snapping at people, losing patience faster than you used to, and feeling vaguely angry at everything — that's not a character flaw. Here's what's actually going on.
always-irritable-burnout.hero_img_alt: Man expressing frustration and irritability from stress and burnout
always-irritable-burnout.label: Anger · Nervous System · Burnout
always-irritable-burnout.h1_after: It's Not Who You Are — It's Your Nervous System
always-irritable-burnout.cta_body: If what you read landed somewhere real, let's talk. One honest conversation can shift more than six months of doing it alone.

content.text: There's a moment most men don't admit to themselves — when you look at a reaction you just had and think, "that's not who I used to be." You snapped at someone. You dismissed something that deserved patience. You felt vaguely furious about nothing in particular, and you can't really explain why. If you're always irritable and it's been building for months, this article is about what's actually happening underneath that — and why anger management is the wrong frame entirely.

The men I work with — founders, executives, high-performing professionals across Europe — often describe a version of this: a short fuse that appeared gradually, usually during a sustained high-pressure period, and then just stayed. They reclassify it as "low tolerance for incompetence" or "being more direct." Sometimes their teams or partners name it first. That's usually when they start paying attention.
What Irritability Actually Is

Irritability from stress isn't an anger problem. It's a nervous system problem that shows up as anger. Here's the distinction: a genuine anger problem is about the relationship to anger as an emotion — how it's triggered, what it means, how it's expressed. What most high-performers are dealing with is something different: a nervous system running in a state of chronic low-grade threat-response, where everything feels slightly more dangerous, more urgent, and more personally threatening than it actually is.

In that state, the threshold for activation drops dramatically. Things that used to require a significant trigger — a late delivery, a miscommunication, a slow queue at a café — now fire the same stress response that previously took much more to produce. Research on stress and emotional reactivity consistently shows this: it's not that stressed people are angrier as a disposition. It's that their system is already partially activated, so the gap to a full stress response becomes very small.
"The anger isn't the issue. It's the signal. The question is what it's signalling."
Why This Hits High-Performers Especially Hard

High-performance environments ask you to suppress your internal state. You don't show overwhelm in a board meeting. You don't let the team see that you're running on four hours of sleep and anxiety. You perform composure while the actual stress accumulates underneath. This is the double bind: the professional skills that make you effective — emotional regulation under pressure, maintaining composure, performing certainty — become the very mechanism through which emotional dysregulation in high performers builds without release.

The suppressed stress has to go somewhere. Often it surfaces at the edges — at home, in traffic, in the gap between calls when nobody's watching. Your partner notices before you do. Your kids notice. And the shame that comes with seeing your own reaction — "I shouldn't have said that, I'm better than this" — adds another layer of tension to a system that's already full.
The Relationship Cost

This is the part that usually lands hardest. The short temper from stress isn't evenly distributed. It comes out most intensely in the places that feel safest — which usually means home. The people closest to you get the worst of a system that's been performing control all day, every day.

Partners describe this as "walking on eggshells." You become someone to manage rather than someone to be with. The relationship starts to feel strategic — what to say, when to raise things, what to avoid. And slowly, the intimacy and ease that made the relationship sustaining starts to erode. Not because of a dramatic event, but because of accumulated months of someone who was present but hard to reach. If you recognise this pattern, the article on work stress affecting relationships goes deeper on the specific dynamic.
You don't need to manage your anger.
content.highlight: You need to discharge the pressure behind it.

content.text: How to Actually Address It

The conventional prescription — anger management, breathing exercises in the moment, counting to ten — addresses the symptom without touching the source. These tools have a place, but applied alone, they're asking someone who's carrying too much pressure to simply contain it better. The pressure remains. The container gets slightly more reinforced. And eventually, something else breaks.

items.text: Not to judge it — to understand it. What situations trigger the response? What does the internal state feel like before the snap? Mapping the pattern is the prerequisite for changing it.

Physical movement is one of the most effective ways to metabolise the stress hormones driving the activation. A 20-minute walk after a difficult meeting achieves more than ten minutes of forcing calm breathing at your desk.

items.strong: Create a gap between end-of-work and home-arrival.
items.text: The transition between the two states is where a lot of the bleed happens. Even fifteen minutes of intentional decompression — a walk, silence, movement — shifts the state you arrive in.

items.strong: Address the chronic stress, not just the moments.
items.text: All of the above helps. But if the underlying system is running on sustained overload — if the burnout signs are present — the reactive irritability is a symptom, not a root cause.

content.text: If you want to work on this with support — not anger management, but actual nervous system regulation work — you can see how I approach this in the work I do with clients.

work-stress-relationship-tension.meta_title: Work Stress Destroying Your Relationship? Here's Why | Johnny Durán
work-stress-relationship-tension.meta_description: Your partner isn't overreacting. When work stress starts bleeding into your relationship, it's a sign something deeper needs addressing. Here's the honest guide.
work-stress-relationship-tension.hero_img_alt: Couple sitting back to back showing distance and relationship tension from work stress
work-stress-relationship-tension.label: Relationships · Stress · Leadership
work-stress-relationship-tension.cta_body: If what you read landed somewhere real, let's talk. One honest conversation can shift more than six months of doing it alone.

content.text: Work stress affecting relationships follows a remarkably consistent pattern. You're building something — a business, a career, a version of success that looks clear from the outside. And simultaneously, something you value just as much — your relationship, your presence at home, your ability to actually be there — is quietly eroding. Not because you stopped caring. Because the resources you'd normally bring to that connection are being consumed elsewhere, and the deficit shows up at home before it shows up anywhere else.

I've worked with enough high-performing men in Barcelona and across Europe to recognise this pattern immediately. They come to me describing work problems — focus, clarity, decision fatigue. And somewhere in the first conversation, the relationship dimension surfaces. A partner who says "you're here but you're not here." Arguments about things that don't really matter. An increasing sense of distance that neither person knows how to close.
The Brilliant-at-Work, Absent-Everywhere-Else Pattern

High-performers are often at their most capable and engaged professionally precisely when they're most depleted relationally. This isn't a coincidence. When your cognitive and emotional bandwidth is being consumed by work at scale — complex decisions, leadership pressure, financial responsibility — what remains for your relationship is the residue. Not the best of you. The leftovers.

Research on emotional resource depletion under work stress shows this clearly: the same regulatory effort that makes you effective professionally depletes your capacity for the kind of warm, attentive, emotionally available presence that relationships require. It's not about effort or intention. It's about resource allocation.
"You can be physically present and completely emotionally unavailable. Your partner knows the difference, even if you don't."
The 4 Ways Stress Corrodes Relationships
1. Withdrawal

The first thing to go is initiative. You stop reaching out, asking questions, showing curiosity about the other person's day. Not out of indifference — out of depletion. You have nothing left to give attention with. Your partner interprets this as distance or disinterest. You don't notice you've withdrawn because you're too focused on survival. The gap widens silently.
2. Irritability

Covered in more depth in the article on irritability and burnout, but the core dynamic is this: a nervous system running in chronic activation has a lower threshold for everything. The person who loves you most is also the person you're safest to be frustrated with. The emotional regulation you maintain all day at work gets applied to your partner as the leftover budget.
3. Transactional Relating

Relationships require a certain amount of non-instrumental attention — time that isn't optimised for anything, where you're just present together. Under high stress, everything becomes optimised. You show up for the practical things — the logistics, the decisions, the plans — but the warmth, play, and spontaneity that make a relationship feel alive start to disappear. You become an effective operational partner. Less so a connected human one.
4. Inability to Receive

This one surprises people. High-stress people often can't let comfort land. A partner offers warmth, support, reassurance — and it slides off, because the defensive, self-reliant state that work stress activates doesn't know how to receive care. You might feel vaguely suspicious of it ("what does she want?"), or dismissive of it ("I don't need that right now"). The result is that your partner stops offering, and the emotional disconnection deepens from both directions.
Relationship tension is usually a
content.highlight: stress problem wearing a domestic disguise.

content.text: Why Fixing the Relationship Doesn't Fix the Problem

This is important enough to say directly: if the problem is work stress causing relationship tension, couples therapy is often addressing the wrong level. The arguments, the distance, the communication failures — these are symptoms. The root is a depleted, stressed individual who doesn't have the internal resources to show up for connection. Working on communication skills when the underlying resource problem isn't addressed is like patching cracks in a wall that's still settling. It doesn't hold.
The Sequence That Addresses This

items.text: "I've been distant" is a description. "I've been running chronically depleted and it's affecting my ability to be present" is a diagnosis. The latter opens a path; the former just creates guilt.

items.strong: Reduce the load at the source.
items.text: Not by abandoning ambition — by addressing how the current load is structured. Chronic stress affecting performance isn't a sustainable operating mode. What's driving it needs examining.

Trying to be more present when you're depleted is effortful and short-lived. The more sustainable path is to increase your capacity first — regulate the nervous system, recover genuine downtime — and then reinvest that capacity into the relationship.
Not the apology conversation. The honest one: "Here's what's actually been happening for me. Here's what I'm doing about it." Partners can meet you a long way if they know what they're meeting.

content.text: A Note on Asking for Help

Most high-performing men don't seek support until something expensive breaks — a relationship crisis, a health event, a business crisis caused by sustained dysfunction. By then, the cost is much higher than it needed to be. The version of this that most of the men I work with arrived at too late: "I wish I'd paid attention to this six months earlier."

Asking for help isn't a retreat from the performance you've built. It's the same investment logic you'd apply to anything else in your life — getting the right support, at the right time, to maintain and extend the asset. In this case, the asset is you, and by extension, everything you're building. If you'd like to understand how I work with this, you can see the approach in the method section, or simply reach out directly.
